docs.title: Option A: Zero Tool Installation (Pre-Packaged Docker Image)
docs.text:
No local terraform, kubectl, helm, or kind required:

docker run --rm -it \
  -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
  -v $(pwd):/workspace \
  -w /workspace \
  ghcr.io/kadhiravaneg/secure-kube:latest \
  make deploy

docs.title: Option B: Local CLI
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/KADHIRAVANEG/secure-kube.git
cd secure-kube
make deploy

In under 5 minutes, you have a 3-node Kubernetes cluster with 7 active defense layers, zero-trust network isolation, and runtime eBPF monitoring.

docs.title: Active Threat Defense & Pod Quarantine
docs.text:
SecureKube transforms traditional runtime security from passive logging into active, zero-trust automated enforcement.

Using the official Falco Talon response engine integrated with Falco's modern eBPF driver, the cluster detects in-flight exploitation and terminates compromised workloads or isolates them into network quarantine within milliseconds.

docs.title: 🏗️ Architecture
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Attacker as Compromised Workload / Attacker
    participant Kernel as Linux Kernel (eBPF)
    participant Falco as Falco DaemonSet
    participant Sidekick as FalcoSidekick
    participant Talon as Falco Talon Controller
    participant K8sAPI as Kubernetes API Server

    Attacker->>Kernel: Spawns interactive shell (execve /bin/sh)
    Kernel-->>Falco: Captures syscall event via modern eBPF probe
    Falco->>Falco: Evaluates rule: "Terminal shell in container"
    Falco->>Sidekick: Emits structured JSON alert (Priority: Notice)
    Sidekick->>Talon: POST http://falco-talon:2803
    Talon->>Talon: Matches rule "Terminal Shell Active Defense"
    Talon->>K8sAPI: DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{pod} (gracePeriodSeconds=0)
    K8sAPI-->>Attacker: SIGKILL sent — Pod immediately evicted
    Talon->>K8sAPI: Emits audit event into Kubernetes Events

docs.title: ⚙️ Configuration & Remediation Rules
docs.text:
Falco Talon is configured via helm/falco-talon-values.yaml. Rules combine actions with pattern matching on Falco event tags and rule names:

config:
  watchRules: true
  deduplication:
    leaderElection: false
    timeWindowSeconds: 5

  rulesOverride: |
    # Action 1: Terminate the compromised pod immediately
    - action: Terminate Compromised Pod
      actionner: kubernetes:terminate
      parameters:
        grace_period_seconds: 0
        ignore_daemonsets: true
        ignore_statefulsets: false

    # Action 2: Apply zero-trust network quarantine label
    - action: Quarantine Suspicious Pod
      actionner: kubernetes:label
      parameters:
        labels:
          security.securekube.io/quarantine: "true"

    # Rule 1: Rogue terminal shell inside container -> Immediate pod termination
    - rule: Terminal Shell Active Defense
      description: "Terminate any pod where an interactive terminal shell is executed"
      match:
        rules:
          - "Terminal shell in container"
        namespaces:
          not:
            - kube-system
            - falco
            - gatekeeper-system
            - monitoring
            - argocd
            - calico-system
            - external-secrets
      actions:
        - Terminate Compromised Pod

    # Rule 2: Credential theft or sensitive file read -> Quarantine & Terminate
    - rule: Sensitive File Access Defense
      description: "Terminate any pod reading sensitive credentials or host files"
      match:
        rules:
          - "Read sensitive file untrusted"
          - "Write below etc"
        namespaces:
          not:
            - kube-system
            - falco
            - gatekeeper-system
            - monitoring
            - argocd
            - calico-system
            - external-secrets
      actions:
        - Quarantine Suspicious Pod
        - Terminate Compromised Pod

docs.title: Run Active Defense Verification
docs.text:
SecureKube provides a dedicated automated verification test (make test-active-defense):

make test-active-defense

This test: 1. Deploys a compliant pod in the default namespace. 2. Simulates an unauthorized interactive terminal execution (sh -c 'uname -a'). 3. Verifies that Falco captures the event via eBPF, dispatches to Talon via FalcoSidekick, and terminates the container. 4. Asserts that the workload enters Terminating or deleted state automatically.

docs.title: Why anonymous-auth is NOT disabled on the API server
docs.text:
CIS control 1.2.1 recommends --anonymous-auth=false. We tried exactly that, and it breaks cluster bootstrap entirely: kubeadm join's default discovery mechanism reads the cluster-info ConfigMap in kube-public unauthenticated — by design, since a joining node has no credentials yet. Disabling anonymous auth makes that read return 401 Unauthorized, and every worker join hangs indefinitely retrying against a wall the cluster itself put up.

This is a genuine, known tension between that CIS control and kubeadm's token-based bootstrap flow, not a misconfiguration on our end. The realistic fixes are: (a) leave anonymous-auth enabled, as we do here, and rely on RBAC + NodeRestriction to constrain what an anonymous/unauthenticated request can actually see or do; or (b) switch to file-based discovery (baking a static bootstrap kubeconfig into worker nodes ahead of time) instead of token discovery, which doesn't need the anonymous ConfigMap read at all. We chose (a) for this project since it keeps make deploy a true one-command flow — (b) would need per-node kubeconfig provisioning as an extra step. If you need anonymous-auth=false for a compliance requirement, implement (b) and update this doc.

docs.title: Why the Terraform layer shells out to the kind CLI instead of using the tehcyx/kind provider
docs.text: We started with the tehcyx/kind Terraform provider's native kind_config resource block. In practice it repeatedly failed to complete multi-node worker joins when combined with custom kubeadm_config_patches — the underlying kind create cluster process would run, but visibility into why it stalled was opaque (Terraform just shows "Still creating..." with no intermediate output). Switching main.tf to a null_resource + local-exec that calls kind create cluster --config kind-config.yaml directly gives the exact same real-time output you'd get running kind by hand — which is what let us find the anonymous-auth issue above in the first place. The trade-off is losing Terraform's native resource semantics (typed attributes, terraform plan diffing on cluster properties); for a project whose value is the security config layered on top, not the provisioning mechanism itself, that trade-off was worth it.

docs.title: Why default-deny + Calico on kind
docs.text: kindnet (kind's default CNI) does not enforce NetworkPolicy — it provides pod networking only. Without swapping in a policy-aware CNI, the default-deny-all NetworkPolicy in kustomize/base/network-policies/ would be silently ignored and the cluster would look zero-trust without being zero-trust. terraform/kind/main.tf disables the default CNI and installs Calico for this reason.

docs.title: Why two enforcement layers (PSA + Gatekeeper)
docs.text:
• Pod Security Admission (PSA), applied via namespace labels, is built into Kubernetes core, has zero extra moving parts, and enforces the standard "restricted" profile.
  • OPA Gatekeeper adds enforcement Kubernetes' native PSA can't express as precisely (e.g. exact rego conditions, custom messages, audit trail of violations over time, extensibility for future org-specific rules).

Together: PSA is the floor that can never regress even if Gatekeeper is ever uninstalled; Gatekeeper is the layer that gives auditable, extensible policy-as-code.

docs.title: Why RBAC ships a workload-runtime Role instead of relying only on defaults
docs.text: Kubernetes ships no default namespaced role suitable for application workloads — teams either bind cluster-admin (too broad) or write nothing (pods run with only their ServiceAccount's implicit, minimal permissions, which usually breaks introspection features). workload-runtime is the least-privilege middle ground: read-only access to configmaps and pod listing, explicitly no secrets access. Secrets access is intentionally left to a separate, per-secret scoped role so it's an explicit decision, not a default.

docs.title: Why the webhook is fail-open (Ignore), not fail-closed (Fail) — corrected
docs.text:
We initially set validatingWebhookFailurePolicy: Fail (see the now-outdated reasoning below) but hit a real, reproducible deadlock on kind+Calico: Calico's IP address management uses cluster-scoped CRDs (IPAMBlock, BlockAffinity) that have no namespace at all. Gatekeeper's own gatekeeper-system exclusion works by namespace label/name — which simply cannot apply to a resource that has no namespace. The result: every pod's IP allocation, in every namespace, calls Gatekeeper's webhook regardless of the exclusion. If that webhook is ever unreachable — including during Gatekeeper's own first install, before its pods have networking yet — no pod anywhere can start, which means Gatekeeper's own pods can never come up to start serving the webhook again. A genuine, unrecoverable deadlock, not a timing fluke.

Switching to Ignore breaks that deadlock: if the webhook is down, requests proceed unvalidated rather than hanging forever. The real cost is a brief enforcement gap any time the webhook pod restarts (e.g. after a node reboot, before Kubernetes reschedules it) — worth knowing if you're relying on this for a real security boundary, not just a demo/portfolio cluster. If you need genuinely fail-closed behavior, the correct fix is upstream: exclude Gatekeeper's own namespace from Calico's admission-relevant object creation entirely (a Calico/Gatekeeper compatibility concern, not something this project's config can fully solve on its own).

docs.title: Compensating Control: Native In-Tree CEL Admission Policies (ValidatingAdmissionPolicy)
docs.text: To eliminate the brief enforcement gap caused by Gatekeeper's fail-open webhook and eliminate external webhook latency (50–200ms per admission request), SecureKube introduces Kubernetes 1.30+ in-tree CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicies in kustomize/base/vap/.

docs.title: The In-Tree vs. Webhook Architecture
docs.text:
Incoming Request -> [ kube-apiserver ]
                         |
                         +---> 1. In-Tree CEL Evaluation (Sub-millisecond, In-Process)
                         |        [vap-no-privileged, vap-no-root, vap-readonly-rootfs, etc.]
                         |        (Rejects immediately if non-compliant; ZERO network roundtrips)
                         |
                         +---> 2. External Webhook Evaluation (Out-of-Process over HTTPS)
                                  [Gatekeeper Webhook Service]
                                  (Deep Rego inspection, Cosign signatures, violation auditing)

docs.title: Key Architectural Advantages:
docs.text:
1. Zero External Network Hops: Evaluated in-memory inside kube-apiserver, slashing admission latency from >100ms down to microseconds.
  2. Zero Webhook Deadlock Risk: Because CEL policies execute in-process, they never deadlock against CNI IPAM CRDs or webhook pod cold-starts.
  3. Dual-Layer Defense: CEL acts as an instantaneous in-tree filter for core security constraints, while Gatekeeper provides extensible Rego policies, comprehensive audit logging (gatekeeper_violations), and Cosign signature verification.

docs.title: Why the Gatekeeper layer has 9 constraints, not 3
docs.text:
The first pass only blocked root/privileged/writable-rootfs — a real attacker doesn't need any of those if hostPath mounting / is left open, or if a pod can set hostNetwork: true and see every other pod's traffic on the node. The current set closes the highest-value gaps beyond what PSA's "restricted" profile alone covers:

Constraint What it stops no-root / no-privileged / readonly-rootfs container escape via root or writable host-equivalent access no-hostpath reading/writing the node filesystem directly no-host-namespaces seeing/signaling every process on the node, or sniffing node network traffic require-resources noisy-neighbor DoS from unbounded pods allowed-repos pulling arbitrary/untrusted images capabilities-and-ports capability creep and binding privileged ports like a root process require-signed-images untrusted supply-chain deployments lacking Cosign cryptographic signatures

This provides comprehensive admission hardening — combined with per-workload egress NetworkPolicies and Falco eBPF runtime observability.

docs.title: Why kube-bench runs in kube-system, not default
docs.text:
The first version of this Makefile applied kube-bench's job manifest without specifying a namespace, so it landed in default — which has pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted from kustomize/base/pod-security/psa-labels.yaml. kube-bench needs hostPID: true and several hostPath volume mounts (it inspects node-level config files like /etc/kubernetes, /var/lib/kubelet, /var/lib/etcd) to do its job at all — every one of those is exactly what the restricted profile blocks. The result: the Job object gets created fine (Jobs aren't subject to Pod Security Admission, only the Pods they spawn are), but every Pod the Job tries to create gets silently rejected, so the Job never has a running Pod and kubectl wait --for=condition=complete times out waiting for something that can never happen. Our own hardening was — correctly — blocking the tool whose entire purpose is to check that hardening.

Fix: run kube-bench in kube-system instead, which we deliberately left unlabeled (no PSA, and already excluded from every Gatekeeper constraint's excludedNamespaces) precisely because cluster-level system tooling legitimately needs broader access than application workloads. This is the same reasoning that already applies to Calico and Gatekeeper's own pods — kube-bench just needed the same treatment and we'd missed it.

docs.title: Why local-path-storage is excluded in Gatekeeper constraints
docs.text:
Kind clusters rely on Rancher's local-path-provisioner to dynamically provision local PersistentVolumes. When a PVC is created (e.g. for Prometheus, Grafana, or Alertmanager), the provisioner spins up a transient helper-pod in the local-path-storage namespace. This helper pod mounts the node's /var/local-path-provisioner directory via hostPath to initialize storage paths, and runs as a minimal utility without explicit resource requests.

If local-path-storage is not explicitly added to excludedNamespaces on Gatekeeper constraints, block-hostpath and require-resources will reject the helper pod on admission. The PVC remains stuck in Pending indefinitely with event logs citing admission rejection. Adding local-path-storage ensures local volume provisioning functions smoothly while keeping all user and workload namespaces strictly enforced.

docs.title: GitOps Architecture: Multi-Application Decoupling
docs.text:
Argo CD manages each layer of SecureKube as a distinct Application object under an AppProject (gitops/apps/project.yaml):

  1. Infrastructure Controllers: calico-system-app, gatekeeper-system-app, falco-system-app.
  2. Cluster Policies: gatekeeper-templates-app, gatekeeper-constraints-app, network-policies-app, pod-security-app, rbac-app.
  3. Workload Reference: secure-app.

To prevent resource ownership conflicts and duplicate drift calculations in Argo CD, each policy layer is maintained in its own self-contained directory with an independent kustomization.yaml (e.g., kustomize/base/network-policies/, kustomize/base/pod-security/, kustomize/base/rbac/). Pointing multiple Argo CD applications at the same directory is strictly avoided.

docs.title: Observability & Security Telemetry Integration
docs.text:
Security without observability creates an operational blind spot. SecureKube combines runtime kernel telemetry with admission audit metrics:

  • Falco eBPF Probes: Inspect system calls (execve, open, connect) on worker and control-plane nodes. Alerts are emitted in JSON to standard out and forwarded over HTTP to falco-sidekick and Redis.
  • Falco Sidekick UI: Visualizes runtime threat frequency, priority classifications (Warning, Error, Critical), and offending container metadata at localhost:2802.
  • Prometheus & Grafana (kube-prometheus-stack): Scrapes Gatekeeper metrics (gatekeeper_violations, gatekeeper_constraints), cAdvisor, and node-exporter metrics. Pre-provisioned dashboards in observability/dashboards/ offer immediate situational awareness of cluster compliance and resource health.

docs.title: Audit logging scope
docs.text: terraform/kind/audit-policy.yaml logs full request/response bodies only for secrets, configmaps, and RBAC objects — the resources where a full body matters for a security investigation — and only request metadata for everything else, to keep log volume manageable while still satisfying CIS 3.2.x.

docs.title: Enterprise Secret Management: SOPS+Age vs. External Secrets Operator (ESO)
docs.text: SecureKube provides two complementary, production-grade secrets patterns tailored to different operational environments:

docs.title: 1. Developer Workstation & Local GitOps: Mozilla SOPS + Age
docs.text:
• Use Case: Local development, CI/CD pipelines, and standalone GitOps repositories without enterprise vault infrastructure.
  • Mechanism: The repository contains .sops.yaml with public Age recipient keys. Secret manifests are encrypted client-side (make secrets-encrypt). Sensitive payload data is encrypted via AES-256-GCM while metadata remains intact for Git versioning. Decryption happens on-the-fly (make secrets-apply) or in-cluster via the KSOPS plugin.

docs.title: 2. Multi-Cloud & Enterprise Vault Sync: External Secrets Operator (ESO)
docs.text:
• Use Case: Enterprise production clusters where developers should never handle encryption keys or decrypt raw secrets on their laptops.
  • Mechanism: ESO runs in-cluster (helm/external-secrets-values.yaml) with a hardened, non-root pod specification. A ClusterSecretStore connects directly to upstream secret providers:
  • Local/CI: fake provider with zero external dependencies and zero cloud billing.
  • AWS: AWS Secrets Manager authenticated via IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA).
  • GCP: GCP Secret Manager authenticated via Workload Identity.
  • On-Premise / Multi-Cloud: HashiCorp Vault authenticated via Kubernetes ServiceAccount tokens.
  • Dynamic Rotation: ESO polls upstream vaults at configured intervals (e.g., refreshInterval: 1h) and automatically synchronizes Kubernetes Secret objects, decoupling secret lifecycle from Git commits.

docs.title: NetworkPolicy Auto-Discovery: Overcoming the Zero-Trust Blackhole
docs.text:
Default-deny networking is the gold standard of zero-trust Kubernetes security, but it often frustrates developers: when a pod is blocked by a NetworkPolicy, packets drop silently without error messages. Applications fail with cryptic i/o timeout or Connection refused errors.

To solve this operational friction, SecureKube implements a two-fold solution: 1. Calico Dropped Packet Observability: Calico Felix Prometheus metrics are exported on port 9091, enabling real-time monitoring of dropped packet counters in Prometheus and Grafana. 2. Automated Discovery & Generator (scripts/generate-network-policy.sh): Rather than guessing egress rules, developers run make generate-network-policy POD=<name>. The generator: - Queries live container specs and runtime ports. - Extracts existing pod labels for targeted podSelector matching. - Automatically injects mandatory CoreDNS egress (UDP/TCP port 53 to kube-dns). - Produces a minimal, least-privilege NetworkPolicy ready for immediate application or commit into GitOps.

docs.title: Automated Workload Hardening Architecture
docs.text: Rather than rejecting non-compliant manifests at admission and forcing developers through frustrating trial-and-error cycles, SecureKube provides an automated manifest transformer (scripts/harden-manifest.py).

docs.title: Design Principles:
docs.text:
• Preserve Developer Intent: Uses PyYAML to load manifests as structured trees, mutating only the necessary fields while preserving custom labels, annotations, volume mounts, and container arguments.
  • Complete AST Injection: Automatically injects all 12 required securityContext fields:
  • Pod: runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001, runAsGroup: 10001, fsGroup: 10001, seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault.
  • Container: allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities.drop: ["ALL"].
  • Resources: sensible default requests (cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi) and limits (cpu: 200m, memory: 128Mi).
  • Privileged Port Remapping: Identifies reserved ports (< 1024) like 80 or 443 and remaps them to unprivileged equivalents (8080, 8443) to prevent CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE privilege escalation.
  • Scratch Space Emulation: Automatically attaches an in-memory emptyDir volume at /tmp so read-only root filesystems don't break applications requiring temporary write space.

docs.title: Smaller lessons worth keeping
docs.text:
• helm/falco-values.yaml uses driver.kind: modern_ebpf, not ebpf. Falco's chart renamed this value; the old name now fails install outright with a clear error, so this is a one-line fix if you ever see it again on a chart upgrade.
  • If a YAML file ever fails kubectl apply with a generic, low-information error (invalid object to validate, json: cannot unmarshal string into Go value of type unstructured.detector) even though the same content parses fine with a YAML linter, suspect file corruption from copy/paste or a transfer step, not a real schema issue — rewriting the file cleanly is often faster than debugging the parser.
  • kubectl's local schema cache (~/.kube/cache) can go stale right after installing a new CRD (e.g. Gatekeeper's ConstraintTemplate). If kubectl apply rejects a resource that looks structurally correct, rm -rf ~/.kube/cache before assuming the YAML itself is wrong.

docs.text: All notable changes to SecureKube are documented here. Format follows Keep a Changelog. Versioning follows Semantic Versioning.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:

The workflow verifies that 8/8 real-world cyber attack scenarios (privilege escalation, host escapes, hostNetwork MITM, untrusted registry supply chain, privileged port hijacking, memory exhaustion DoS, Calico lateral pivoting, and Falco eBPF runtime exploitation) are actively blocked or detected with a 100% defense score, failing the build on any breach.

docs.title: Code of conduct
docs.text: Be respectful, constructive, and patient. We're all here to learn and build something useful. Harassment of any kind is not tolerated.

docs.title: What we're looking for
docs.text:
Good contributions include:

  • Bug fixes — especially around cluster provisioning, policy enforcement, or CI reliability
  • New Gatekeeper constraints — additional security controls with corresponding tests
  • Cloud modules — EKS, GKE, or AKS Terraform modules following the same pattern as terraform/kind/
  • Documentation improvements — clarifying the architecture, adding examples, fixing inaccuracies
  • Test coverage — more negative/positive test cases in scripts/test-policies.sh
  • Tooling improvements — better observability, dashboards, or developer experience

We are NOT currently looking for:

  • Changes that weaken the default security posture without a strong justification
  • Additions that require a paid cloud account to test
  • Large rewrites without prior discussion in an issue

docs.title: Testing requirements
docs.text:
Every PR that changes a policy, constraint, script, or security control must:

  • Pass offline policy validation: make test-offline (gator test v3.18.0)

  • Pass the security assault simulation: make attack (all 8 attack vectors repelled)
  • Pass CI (GitHub Actions runs automatically on every PR)

For new Gatekeeper constraints specifically: - Add the ConstraintTemplate in gatekeeper/constraint-templates/ with enriched remediation guidance - Add the Constraint in gatekeeper/constraints/ with argocd, gatekeeper-system, falco, kube-system, calico-system, monitoring, local-path-storage, external-secrets in excludedNamespaces - If applicable, add a corresponding native in-tree CEL ValidatingAdmissionPolicy in kustomize/base/vap/ - Add a negative test pod in examples/insecure-apps.yaml - Add the pod name to the EXPECTED_REJECTED list in scripts/test-policies.sh - Document the threat vector mitigated in docs/architecture.md

docs.title: Zero-Trust Networking & Microsegmentation
docs.text: SecureKube implements a strict zero-trust network model powered by Project Calico CNI. By default, all network traffic is dropped unless an explicit, least-privilege NetworkPolicy allows it.

docs.title: 🔒 Default-Deny Architecture
docs.text:
The cluster ships with a cluster-wide default-deny policy in kustomize/base/network-policies/default-deny.yaml:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-all
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
    - Egress

docs.title: What Default-Deny Blocks
docs.text:
Without an explicit allow policy: - ❌ Pods cannot perform DNS queries to CoreDNS. - ❌ Pods cannot communicate with other workloads in the same or other namespaces. - ❌ Pods cannot initiate outbound egress to external APIs or the internet. - ❌ Lateral pivoting after a container breakout is rendered impossible at the packet layer.

To enable essential cluster functionality, SecureKube provisions an isolated DNS egress policy:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53

docs.title: 🤖 Automated NetworkPolicy Discovery Tool
docs.text:
One of the greatest developer pain points is figuring out exact egress ports and IP ranges required by a microservice.

SecureKube solves this with scripts/generate-network-policy.sh:

make generate-network-policy TARGET=my-app-pod NS=default

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Analyzes live socket connections and /proc/net tables of the running target pod.
  2. Identifies all remote endpoints and destination ports.
  3. Classifies endpoints into:
  4. Internal Cluster Services: Translates Service ClusterIPs to Kubernetes Service selectors.
  5. External Public Endpoints: Translates external CIDRs into scoped IPBlocks.
  6. Auto-generates a ready-to-apply, least-privilege YAML manifest:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: my-app-discovered-egress
  namespace: default
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: my-app
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    # Discovered DNS dependency
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
    # Discovered PostgreSQL dependency
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: postgresql
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 5432

docs.text:
When a developer or operator performs an ad-hoc kubectl edit or kubectl apply outside Git, Argo CD marks the application as OutOfSync. You can inspect the exact diff in the Argo CD web console at http://localhost:8080 or via CLI:

docs.title: 4. Authoring Compliant Workloads
docs.text: To deploy an application successfully onto SecureKube, the pod manifest must adhere to Pod Security Standards (restricted) and all 9 OPA Gatekeeper constraints:

docs.title: Workload Checklist:
docs.text:
• [x] Run as a non-root user (runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001)
  • [x] Disallow privilege escalation (allowPrivilegeEscalation: false)
  • [x] Drop all capabilities except explicitly permitted (drop: ["ALL"])
  • [x] Mount root filesystem read-only (readOnlyRootFilesystem: true)
  • [x] Set explicit CPU and Memory requests and limits
  • [x] Use seccomp profile RuntimeDefault
  • [x] Pull images only from approved registries (docker.io/library/, ghcr.io/, gcr.io/, registry.k8s.io/)
  • [x] Never use hostPath, hostNetwork, hostPID, or hostIPC
  • [x] Bind only to non-privileged ports (> 1024)

docs.title: Reference Compliant Pod
docs.text:
See examples/secure-app.yaml for a fully annotated production-grade template:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-secure-app
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: my-secure-app
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    runAsGroup: 10001
    fsGroup: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: docker.io/library/nginx:alpine
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
      resources:
        limits:
          cpu: "200m"
          memory: "128Mi"
        requests:
          cpu: "50m"
          memory: "64Mi"

docs.title: 5. Runtime Security & Falco Threat Hunting
docs.text: Falco observes kernel events across all nodes using the modern eBPF driver.

docs.title: Live Threat Monitoring
docs.text:
Tail live alerts stream: 

make logs

docs.title: Simulating a Runtime Security Violation
docs.text:
To test that Falco accurately detects unauthorized behavior in a container:

# 1. Spawn a compliant test container
kubectl run test-sec --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --command -- sleep 3600

# 2. Exec a terminal shell inside the container (Falco rule: "Terminal shell in container")
kubectl exec -it test-sec -- sh -c "cat /etc/shadow"

# 3. Check Falco alerts:
make logs | grep "Terminal shell"

The event will immediately reflect on the Falco Sidekick UI at http://localhost:2802 categorized as Notice or Warning.

docs.title: 1. PVCs Stuck in Pending
docs.text:
• Symptom: kubectl get pvc -A shows PVCs in Pending state.
  • Cause: Kind's local-path-provisioner helper pod was rejected by admission webhooks.
  • Remediation: Ensure local-path-storage is present in excludedNamespaces in all files in gatekeeper/constraints/.

docs.title: 2. Node in NotReady State
docs.text:
• Symptom: Nodes remain in NotReady after make cluster.
  • Cause: SecureKube disables default kindnet to enforce Calico. The node remains NotReady until a CNI provides network routing.
  • Remediation: Run make policies or kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.27.0/manifests/calico.yaml.

docs.title: 3. Webhook Connection Reset on Local Port-Forward
docs.text:
• Symptom: kubectl port-forward exits with connection reset by peer.
  • Cause: Argo CD runs HTTP on port 8080 (--insecure), but service port 443 routes to the same container port.
  • Remediation: Forward port 80 to 8080 or pod port 8080 directly: 
    kubectl -n argocd port-forward svc/argocd-server 8080:80 --address 127.0.0.1

docs.title: 7. GitOps Secrets Management (SOPS + Age)
docs.text: Storing raw secrets in Git repositories is a critical vulnerability. SecureKube implements zero-trust GitOps secrets management using Mozilla SOPS and modern Age asymmetric encryption.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
1. Local Key Generation: A private/public Age keypair is generated locally (~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt).
  2. Public Key Configuration: The public recipient is committed to .sops.yaml targeting .*\.enc\.ya?ml$.
  3. Encrypted in Git: Kubernetes Secret manifests (e.g., gitops/secrets/database-credentials.enc.yaml) are committed fully encrypted. Only keys and metadata remain plaintext; sensitive payload values are AES-256-GCM encrypted.
  4. On-the-Fly Application: Manifests are decrypted in-memory during application without writing plaintext to disk.

docs.title: Secrets Lifecycle Operations
docs.text:
# 1. Initialize Age keypair & configure .sops.yaml
make secrets-init

# 2. Encrypt an existing plaintext Secret manifest
make secrets-encrypt FILE=my-secret.yaml DEST=gitops/secrets/my-secret.enc.yaml

# 3. Decrypt and apply encrypted secrets directly to the live cluster
make secrets-apply

# 4. Sync Age private key to Argo CD namespace (for GitOps KSOPS plugin)
./scripts/secrets-tool.sh sync-key

docs.title: Reference Pod Consuming Decrypted Secret
docs.text:
See examples/secure-app-with-secret.yaml for a hardened, admitted workload consuming database credentials via environment variables:

kubectl apply -f examples/secure-app-with-secret.yaml
kubectl logs -n default pod/secure-app-with-secret

docs.title: 9. Automated Workload Hardening (make harden)
docs.text: Developers often struggle with the 12+ required securityContext and resource fields required by Gatekeeper and Pod Security Standards. SecureKube includes scripts/harden-manifest.py, an automated AST-based manifest transformer:

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Preview hardened manifest in stdout
make harden FILE=my-insecure-pod.yaml

# Overwrite in-place
make harden FILE=my-insecure-pod.yaml IN_PLACE=true

# Output to a specific file
make harden FILE=my-insecure-pod.yaml OUTPUT=my-hardened-pod.yaml

docs.title: What It Remediates Automatically
docs.text:
• Injects Pod-level runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001, runAsGroup: 10001, fsGroup: 10001, and seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault.
  • Injects Container-level allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, and capabilities.drop: ["ALL"].
  • Injects sensible default resource limits and requests (cpu: 200m/50m, memory: 128Mi/64Mi).
  • Rewrites privileged container ports (e.g. 80 -> 8080, 443 -> 8443) to prevent host port hijacking.
  • Adds an emptyDir scratch volume (/tmp) for read-only root filesystems requiring temp write space.

docs.title: 10. Native In-Tree CEL Admission Policies (ValidatingAdmissionPolicy)
docs.text:
Starting in Kubernetes 1.30, admission control can be executed in-process inside kube-apiserver using Common Expression Language (CEL), bypassing webhook latencies (50–200ms) and avoiding webhook failure deadlocks.

SecureKube deploys 8 native CEL policies located in kustomize/base/vap/: 1. vap-no-privileged: Prohibits securityContext.privileged: true. 2. vap-no-root: Enforces runAsNonRoot: true or non-zero runAsUser. 3. vap-readonly-rootfs: Enforces readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. 4. vap-no-hostpath: Prohibits hostPath volume mounts. 5. vap-no-host-namespaces: Prohibits hostNetwork, hostPID, and hostIPC. 6. vap-require-resources: Enforces CPU and memory requests/limits. 7. vap-capabilities-and-ports: Enforces capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] and port > 1024. 8. vap-allowed-registries: Restricts container image registries to approved sources.

docs.title: Deploying & Testing CEL Policies
docs.text:
# Deploy CEL policies and cluster-wide bindings
make vap

# Policies run in-tree alongside Gatekeeper and evaluate instantaneously
kubectl apply -f examples/insecure-apps.yaml

docs.title: 11. NetworkPolicy Auto-Discovery / Generator (make generate-network-policy)
docs.text: Debugging silent packet drops in zero-trust environments can stall developer velocity. SecureKube includes scripts/generate-network-policy.sh to auto-generate minimal least-privilege egress and ingress rules.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# Discover live ports and generate NetworkPolicy for a pod
make generate-network-policy POD=my-app NAMESPACE=default

docs.title: Generated Policy Properties
docs.text:
• Automatically extracts pod labels and container ports for ingress rules.
  • Automatically includes mandatory egress to CoreDNS (kube-dns on UDP/TCP port 53).
  • Implements strict default-deny for all unauthorized ingress and egress traffic.

docs.title: 12. External Secrets Operator (Local Fake Vault & Enterprise Sync)
docs.text: For enterprise environments using HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or GCP Secret Manager, SecureKube integrates the External Secrets Operator (ESO):

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
• Runs with hardened non-root container specs (helm/external-secrets-values.yaml).
  • Configures ClusterSecretStore (gitops/secrets/eso/cluster-secret-store.yaml).
  • Local environments use the built-in fake provider for zero-cost, zero-dependency testing.
  • Includes pre-configured production blocks for Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, and GCP Secret Manager.

docs.title: Deployment & Verification
docs.text:
# Deploy ESO and synchronize secrets
make secrets-eso

# Verify materialized secret
kubectl get secret database-credentials-vault -n default -o yaml

# Run workload consuming ESO synchronized secret
kubectl apply -f examples/secure-app-with-vault-secret.yaml
kubectl logs -n default pod/secure-app-with-vault-secret

docs.title: 13. Production Cloud Provisioning (AWS EKS & GCP GKE)
docs.text: SecureKube provides production-ready Terraform modules to deploy the identical zero-trust security baseline onto managed hyperscaler cloud environments:

docs.title: AWS EKS (terraform/eks/)
docs.text:

docs.title: Enterprise Secret Management
docs.text: SecureKube provides a dual-layer secret management architecture designed for both local GitOps workflows and multi-cloud enterprise production deployments.

docs.title: 🔀 Two Operational Models
docs.text: Capability Local GitOps (SOPS + Age) Enterprise Vaults (ESO) Primary Tool Mozilla SOPS + Age CLI External Secrets Operator (ESO) Best For Offline development, local Kind clusters, pure GitOps repos Production clouds (AWS, GCP, Vault, Azure) Key Location Developer workstation (~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt) Managed Cloud KMS / IAM Role / Vault AppRole Rotation Manual re-encryption on commit Fully automated polling (refreshInterval: 1h) Developer Overhead Low (single CLI command) Zero (developers never touch raw keys)

docs.title: 🔒 Layer A: Local GitOps via Mozilla SOPS + Age
docs.text: For developer laptops and self-contained repositories, SecureKube integrates SOPS with modern, lightweight Age asymmetric encryption.

docs.title: 1. Initialize Age Keypair
docs.text:
make secrets-init
Generates a 256-bit Age keypair at ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt and automatically generates the .sops.yaml encryption rule binding your repository to the generated public key.

docs.title: 2. Encrypt a Kubernetes Secret
docs.text:
make secrets-encrypt FILE=gitops/secrets/examples/app-secret.yaml
Outputs an encrypted manifest with envelope integrity signatures (.enc.yaml). The ciphertext is completely safe to commit into public Git repositories.

docs.title: 3. Decrypt and Apply On-The-Fly
docs.text:
make secrets-apply
Decrypts the encrypted manifest in-memory and pipes it directly into kubectl apply without writing unencrypted secrets to disk.

docs.title: 🏢 Layer B: Enterprise Secret Synchronization (ESO)
docs.text: For production enterprise environments, SecureKube deploys the External Secrets Operator. Workloads declare an ExternalSecret custom resource, and the operator synchronizes credentials directly into native Kubernetes Secret objects.

docs.title: 1. Install External Secrets Operator
docs.text: make secrets-eso

docs.title: 2. The ExternalSecret Custom Resource
docs.text:
Developers declare what secrets they need without handling credentials:

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: database-credentials
  namespace: default
spec:
  refreshInterval: "1h"
  secretStoreRef:
    name: securekube-vault-store
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
  target:
    name: database-credentials-k8s
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: DB_USER
      remoteRef:
        key: production/database
        property: username
    - secretKey: DB_PASS
      remoteRef:
        key: production/database
        property: password

docs.title: HashiCorp Vault (Kubernetes Auth)
docs.text:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: vault-backend
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: "https://vault.internal.corp:8200"
      path: "secret"
      version: "v2"
      auth:
        kubernetes:
          mountPath: "kubernetes"
          role: "securekube-workload-role"

docs.title: AWS Secrets Manager (IRSA)
docs.text:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secrets-manager
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: eso-irsa-sa
            namespace: external-secrets

docs.title: GCP Secret Manager (Workload Identity)
docs.text:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: gcp-secret-manager
spec:
  provider:
    gcpsm:
      projectID: my-hardened-gcp-project
      auth:
        workloadIdentity:
          clusterLocation: us-central1
          clusterName: securekube-gke
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: eso-wi-sa
            namespace: external-secrets

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Do not open a public GitHub issue for security vulnerabilities.

Report privately via GitHub's built-in security advisory: 1. Go to https://github.com/KADHIRAVANEG/secure-kube/security/advisories 2. Click New draft security advisory 3. Fill in the details and submit

We will respond within 72 hours and aim to release a fix within 14 days for confirmed vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This project is a local development / reference implementation. Please report:

  • Vulnerabilities in the container image (ghcr.io/kadhiravaneg/secure-kube or joker53/secure-kube)
  • Gatekeeper constraints or CEL admission policies that can be bypassed in ways not already documented
  • CI/CD workflow vulnerabilities (secret exposure, injection attacks)
  • Incorrect security documentation that could mislead users into unsafe configurations

Out of scope:

  • CIS benchmark failures on kind that are documented in docs/architecture.md
  • The fail-open Gatekeeper webhook (compensated by in-tree CEL admission policies)
  • Anonymous auth being enabled (documented trade-off)
  • Vulnerabilities in upstream tools (report to Terraform, Gatekeeper, Falco, etc. directly)

docs.title: Known security trade-offs
docs.text:
These are intentional, documented decisions — not vulnerabilities:

Trade-off Reason Reference Gatekeeper webhook is fail-open Calico IPAM deadlock with fail-closed (mitigated by in-tree CEL policies) docs/architecture.md anonymous-auth enabled kubeadm join bootstrap token requires it docs/architecture.md CIS benchmark partially fails kind cannot satisfy node-level controls README.md Permissive allowed-repos list Bundled examples need public registries gatekeeper/constraints/allowed-repos-constraint.yaml local-path-storage excluded from constraints Kind dynamic volume provisioner helper pod requires hostPath docs/architecture.md external-secrets excluded from constraints External Secrets Operator webhook and cert-controller require system permissions docs/architecture.md

docs.title: Supply-Chain Security & SLSA Level 3 Attestation
docs.text: Software supply-chain attacks are among the most pervasive attack vectors facing modern cloud-native systems. SecureKube implements a hardened end-to-end supply-chain pipeline reaching SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) Level 3.

docs.title: 🔒 Pillars of Supply-Chain Security
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Source Code (Git Tag)"] --> B["Multi-Arch Build<br>(AMD64 + ARM64)"]
    B --> C["Syft SPDX SBOM Generation"]
    C --> D["Sigstore Cosign Keyless OIDC Signing"]
    D --> E["Cosign Predicate Attestation"]
    E --> F["Gatekeeper In-Cluster Admission"]

docs.title: 1. Multi-Architecture Support
docs.text: SecureKube produces official multi-architecture container images supporting both linux/amd64 (Intel/AMD) and linux/arm64 (Apple Silicon, AWS Graviton, Ampere): - ghcr.io/kadhiravaneg/secure-kube:<version> - joker53/secure-kube:<version>

docs.title: 2. Sigstore Cosign Keyless Signing
docs.text: Images are cryptographically signed using Sigstore Cosign. Signing is completely keyless, backed by GitHub Actions OpenID Connect (OIDC) workload identity: - No static private keys stored in CI secrets that could be leaked or stolen. - Signatures are tied to the exact Git commit, tag, and GitHub Actions workflow run. - Signatures and transparency logs are written to the public Sigstore Rekor ledger.

docs.title: 3. SPDX Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
docs.text: Every container release automatically generates an SPDX-JSON Software Bill of Materials via Anchore Syft. The SBOM records: - Operating system packages (Debian/Ubuntu baseline) - Upstream binary tool hashes (terraform, kubectl, helm, kind, argocd) - Package licensing, file manifests, and dependencies

docs.title: 4. Cryptographic Attestation
docs.text:
The SBOM is attached directly to the container image registry as an authenticated in-toto predicate using:

cosign attest --yes \
  --predicate sbom.spdx.json \
  --type spdx \
  ghcr.io/kadhiravaneg/secure-kube:<digest>

docs.title: 🔍 How to Verify Signatures & SBOMs
docs.text:
SecureKube provides a built-in verification script to inspect image provenance before deployment:

make verify-sbom

Or run directly against any image tag:

./scripts/verify-sbom.sh ghcr.io/kadhiravaneg/secure-kube:v1.6.0

docs.title: Manual Verification Commands
docs.text: To verify using the cosign CLI manually:

docs.title: 1. Verify Image Signature
docs.text:
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/KADHIRAVANEG/secure-kube/.*" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  ghcr.io/kadhiravaneg/secure-kube:v1.6.0

docs.title: 2. Verify and Download the Attested SBOM
docs.text:
cosign verify-attestation \
  --type spdx \
  --certificate-identity-regexp="https://github.com/KADHIRAVANEG/secure-kube/.*" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer="https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  ghcr.io/kadhiravaneg/secure-kube:v1.6.0 | jq -r '.payload | @base64d | fromjson | .predicate' > sbom.json

docs.title: 🛡️ In-Cluster Gatekeeper Enforcement
docs.text: At admission time, SecureKube's OPA Gatekeeper constraint (require-signed-images-constraint.yaml) verifies that workloads deployed into production namespaces originate from authorized registries and pass image signature verification.

docs.title: AWS EKS CIS-Hardened Deployment
docs.text: SecureKube provides production Terraform scaffolding in terraform/eks to provision an enterprise-grade, CIS-compliant Amazon EKS cluster that enforces the exact same security policies applied in local Kind development.

docs.title: 🛡️ Security Features
docs.text:
1. CIS Control Plane Logging: Automatically streams api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, and scheduler logs to AWS CloudWatch with configurable retention.
  2. KMS Envelope Encryption: All Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted at rest with a dedicated customer-managed AWS KMS key (aws_kms_key.eks).
  3. IMDSv2 Enforced: Worker EC2 nodes require token-based metadata access (http_tokens = "required", http_put_response_hop_limit = 1), defeating SSRF container metadata escape attacks.
  4. IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA): Pre-configured OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider allows least-privilege pod IAM roles without static AWS credentials.
  5. Private API Endpoint: Configurable public/private endpoint access with CIDR block whitelisting.
  6. Automated Baseline Application: Applies the exact same SecureKube NetworkPolicies, least-privilege RBAC, and in-tree CEL admission policies upon cluster completion.

terraform init

# Validate configuration
make cloud-eks

terraform apply -var="vpc_id=vpc-0123456789abcdef0" -var='subnet_ids=["subnet-a", "subnet-b", "subnet-c"]'

docs.title: GCP GKE CIS-Hardened Deployment
docs.text: SecureKube provides production Terraform scaffolding in terraform/gke to provision an enterprise-grade, CIS-compliant Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster.

docs.title: 🛡️ Security Features
docs.text:
1. Datapath V2 (Cilium eBPF): Native, high-performance in-kernel packet filtering with default NetworkPolicy enforcement without iptables overhead.
  2. Workload Identity Federation: Binds Kubernetes ServiceAccounts directly to Google Cloud IAM roles, eliminating long-lived GCP service account keys.
  3. Shielded GKE Nodes: Enforces Secure Boot and node firmware integrity monitoring.
  4. Metadata Concealment: Configures workload_metadata_config.mode = "GKE_METADATA" to prevent container breakouts to Google Cloud Instance Metadata.
  5. Private Cluster: Disables public worker node IPs and protects the control plane with master authorized network CIDRs.
  6. Automated Baseline Application: Applies the exact same SecureKube NetworkPolicies and in-tree CEL admission policies upon cluster completion.
